title: SQL for Application Support
subtitle: Find the data behind the ticket
description: Answer real support questions from a small support database: ticket statuses and priorities, joins to customers and agents, and counts that prove what is happening. Every query runs in the page.

lessons.title: Reading a Support Database
lessons.body:
SQL is how you ask a database a question. Before you can ask anything, you need to know how the data is arranged. A database stores information in **tables**, and a table is just a grid: named **columns** down the side, and one **row** per thing.

This course runs on a small support database with three tables:

| table | one row is... | columns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tickets` | one support ticket | id, subject, status, priority, customer_id, agent_id, resolved_minutes |
| `customers` | one customer account | id, name, plan, region |
| `agents` | one support engineer | id, name, team, level |

Every query starts the same way: what you want, then where it lives.

```sql
SELECT * FROM tickets;
```

Read it aloud: select every column (`*` means all columns) from the tickets table. The result is always a fresh grid holding exactly the columns you asked for. When you only need a few, name them instead, in the order you want them back:

```sql
SELECT subject, status, priority FROM tickets;
```

Order in the `SELECT` list is order in the result, so `subject` is always the first column of the output.

exercises.prompt: Show every column of every ticket.
exercises.hint: The star stands for all columns.
exercises.explain: SELECT * returns every column of every row - the whole tickets table.

exercises.prompt: Show just the subject, status, and priority of each ticket, in that order.
exercises.solution: SELECT subject, status, priority FROM tickets
exercises.hint: Separate the column names with commas, in the order you want them.
exercises.explain: The columns come back exactly as you named them: subject first, then status, then priority.

exercises.prompt: In the `tickets` table, what does one row represent?
options: One support ticket and its details
exercises.explain: One row per ticket. Each column (status, priority, agent_id...) is a property of that ticket.
exercises.hint: Think about the noun the table is named after.

exercises.prompt: Which SQL keyword begins every query that reads data from a table?
exercises.hint: It is the first word of every query in this course.
exercises.explain: SELECT names what you want back; FROM names where it lives.

lessons.title: Filtering with WHERE

exercises.prompt: List the subject and priority of every P1 ticket.
exercises.starter: SELECT subject, priority FROM tickets WHERE
exercises.solution: SELECT subject, priority FROM tickets WHERE priority = 'P1'
exercises.hint: P1 is text, so it needs single quotes.
exercises.explain: Three tickets carry the top priority: ids 1, 6 and 9.

exercises.prompt: List the subject of tickets that are both Open and P1.
exercises.solution: SELECT subject FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Open' AND priority = 'P1'
exercises.hint: Join the two conditions with AND.
exercises.explain: AND keeps only rows where both conditions hold: ticket 1 and ticket 9.

exercises.prompt: List the subject and status of every ticket that is New or Pending - the ones nobody has finished.
exercises.starter: SELECT subject, status FROM tickets WHERE
exercises.solution: SELECT subject, status FROM tickets WHERE status = 'New' OR status = 'Pending'
exercises.hint: OR keeps a row if either side is true.
exercises.explain: Four tickets are New or Pending; the Open and Resolved ones drop out.

exercises.prompt: List the subject of every ticket that is not yet Resolved.
exercises.solution: SELECT subject FROM tickets WHERE NOT status = 'Resolved'
exercises.hint: NOT flips a condition: everything except the matches.
exercises.explain: Seven tickets survive - all of them except the three Resolved ones.

lessons.title: Sorting and Limiting
lessons.body:
A query makes no promise about the order rows come back in. If the order matters, you have to ask for it:

```sql
SELECT id, subject FROM tickets ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 3;
```

`ORDER BY` names the column to sort on. `ASC` means ascending (lowest first) and it is the default when you write nothing. `DESC` means descending (highest first). Ticket ids grow over time, so `ORDER BY id DESC` puts the newest tickets first - a queue view an agent can work straight down.

`LIMIT` keeps only the first N rows of whatever has been produced. Because sorting happens **before** trimming, the pair answers everyday questions: the three newest tickets, the slowest resolutions, the oldest ticket still waiting. Get the clauses in the wrong order and the query is rejected: `FROM`, then `WHERE`, then `ORDER BY`, then `LIMIT`, in that fixed sequence.

exercises.prompt: Show the three newest tickets: their id and subject, newest first.
exercises.solution: SELECT id, subject FROM tickets ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 3
exercises.hint: Sort on id descending, then trim the list with LIMIT 3.
exercises.explain: Ids grow over time, so the highest ids are the newest tickets.

exercises.prompt: List the subjects of all Open tickets, oldest ticket first.
exercises.solution: SELECT subject FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Open' ORDER BY id ASC
exercises.hint: Filter with WHERE first, then sort ascending on id.
exercises.explain: The Open tickets are ids 1, 4 and 9 - ascending id puts the oldest one first.

exercises.prompt: Among Resolved tickets, which ones took longest? Show subject and resolved_minutes, slowest first.
exercises.solution: SELECT subject, resolved_minutes FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Resolved' ORDER BY resolved_minutes DESC
exercises.hint: Filter to Resolved so every row has a number, then sort the minutes descending.
exercises.explain: Descending puts the biggest number - the slowest fix - on top.

exercises.prompt: A query runs in a fixed order. Put these steps in the sequence the database follows
items: Read the table named in FROM
Keep only matching rows with WHERE
Sort the surviving rows with ORDER BY
Trim the list to the first N rows with LIMIT
exercises.explain: FROM, then WHERE, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT - which is why you cannot write LIMIT before ORDER BY.
exercises.hint: Start with where the data comes from, finish with how much of it you keep.

lessons.title: Joining Tables
lessons.body:
Support data is spread across tables so nothing is stored twice. A ticket does not repeat the customer's name; it stores `customer_id`, a number pointing at a row in `customers`. That number is a **foreign key**, and a `JOIN` follows it:

```sql
SELECT tickets.subject, customers.name
FROM tickets
JOIN customers ON tickets.customer_id = customers.id;
```

Read it as: for each ticket row, find the customer row whose `id` equals the ticket's `customer_id`, and stitch the two into one output row. The `ON` clause is the matching rule - get it wrong and you get nonsense, or nothing at all.

Tickets also carry `agent_id`, pointing at `agents`, so the same pattern answers who is handling what:

```sql
SELECT tickets.subject, agents.name
FROM tickets
JOIN agents ON tickets.agent_id = agents.id;
```

Notice the column names in the result: the engine returns bare names - `subject`, `name` - even though you wrote `customers.name`. If two tables both have a column called `id`, qualify it (`tickets.id`) in the query so there is no doubt which one you mean.

exercises.prompt: A ticket row has `customer_id = 4`. What does the 4 refer to?
options: The row in the customers table whose id is 4
The agent assigned to the ticket
exercises.explain: customer_id is a foreign key: it points at customers.id, so it matches one customer's row.
exercises.hint: The number points across the tables.

exercises.prompt: Show each ticket's subject next to the name of the customer who raised it.
exercises.solution: SELECT tickets.subject, customers.name FROM tickets JOIN customers ON tickets.customer_id = customers.id
exercises.hint: JOIN customers ON tickets.customer_id = customers.id
exercises.explain: Ten tickets, each stitched to the customer that raised it.

exercises.prompt: List the subject of every ticket raised by an Enterprise-plan customer.
exercises.starter: SELECT tickets.subject FROM tickets JOIN customers ON tickets.customer_id = customers.id
exercises.solution: SELECT tickets.subject FROM tickets JOIN customers ON tickets.customer_id = customers.id WHERE customers.plan = 'Enterprise'
exercises.hint: Add WHERE customers.plan = 'Enterprise' after the join.
exercises.explain: Northwind Traders and Tailspin Toys are the Enterprise customers - four tickets between them.

exercises.prompt: Show the subject and the handling agent's team for every ticket worked by Ana Novak.
exercises.starter: SELECT tickets.subject, agents.team FROM tickets JOIN agents ON tickets.agent_id = agents.id
exercises.solution: SELECT tickets.subject, agents.team FROM tickets JOIN agents ON tickets.agent_id = agents.id WHERE agents.name = 'Ana Novak'
exercises.hint: Join on tickets.agent_id = agents.id, then filter with WHERE agents.name = 'Ana Novak'.
exercises.explain: Ana Novak is agents.id 4, who handled tickets 6 and 9 - both on the Identity team.

lessons.title: Counting and Summarising
lessons.body:
Sometimes you do not want a list of rows, you want one number. **Aggregate functions** collapse the whole result into a single value:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets;
SELECT AVG(resolved_minutes) FROM tickets;
```

`COUNT(*)` counts rows. `COUNT(column)` counts only the rows where that column actually holds a value, and that difference matters here: unresolved tickets have an empty `resolved_minutes`, which SQL calls **NULL**. So `COUNT(*)` returns 10 while `COUNT(resolved_minutes)` returns 5. `SUM` adds a column up, `MIN` and `MAX` find the ends, and `AVG` is the mean - all of them ignoring NULLs.

Aggregates pair with `WHERE`, because they only see the rows that survived the filter:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Open';
```

The result of an aggregate query is always **one row**, and the column name is the function exactly as written: `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(resolved_minutes)`, `AVG(resolved_minutes)`. There is no `GROUP BY` in this engine, so every aggregate answers about the whole (filtered) table at once.

exercises.prompt: How many tickets are still Open? Show just the count.
exercises.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Open'
exercises.hint: COUNT with a star inside the parentheses, plus a WHERE filter.
exercises.explain: Three tickets - ids 1, 4 and 9 - are still Open.

exercises.prompt: How many tickets already have a resolution time recorded? Show just that count.
exercises.hint: COUNT(column) skips the rows where that column is empty (NULL).
exercises.explain: Ten tickets exist, but only five hold a resolved_minutes value, so COUNT(resolved_minutes) returns 5.

exercises.prompt: What is the average resolution time, in minutes, across the tickets that have one? Show just the average.
exercises.hint: AVG over the resolved_minutes column; it ignores the empty cells.
exercises.explain: 95 + 320 + 45 + 180 + 60 = 700 minutes across 5 tickets, so the average is 140.

exercises.prompt: Name the aggregate function that adds up the values in a numeric column.
exercises.hint: Three letters, and it is what a spreadsheet calls a total.
exercises.explain: SUM adds a column up - for example SELECT SUM(resolved_minutes) FROM tickets returns 700.
